definition: Something shown in a time period where it could not have existed, like a phone in an ancient tale.
example: A typewriter on stage in a play set in 1700 would be a glaring anachronism.
nuance: An anachronism is out of place in time; an anomaly can be odd in any way, and an archaism is old wording used on purpose.
prompt: A historian reviews the costumes in a film set in medieval England.
options: The historian noted that the zipper on the queen's gown was an anachronism.
The historian called the castle an anachronism simply because it was so old and grand.
The historian praised each anachronism for matching the medieval period perfectly.
The historian complained that the anachronism of the film ran nearly three hours.
reasons: Zippers were invented centuries later, so one has no place in a medieval scene.
A castle fits a medieval setting; being ancient is not the same as being in the wrong era.
This reverses the meaning: these errors clash with their period instead of matching it.
A movie's running time is its length, not a detail misplaced in history.

practice.prompt: A student writes a short story about a farm family in the year 1850.
options: In a story set in 1850, the farmer's text message to his neighbor is an anachronism.
The student included an anachronism by giving the 1850 farmer a horse-drawn plow.
The teacher said the story's anachronism was its flashback to the farmer's boyhood.
The student created an anachronism by spelling the farmer's name two different ways.
reasons: Cell phones did not exist in 1850, so the message belongs to a much later era.
Horse-drawn plows were common then, so this detail fits the period.
A flashback is a storytelling technique, not an object from the wrong era.
Spelling a name inconsistently is a typo, not a historical mismatch.
